system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: ocsf_api_activity holds all three clouds normalized to the OCSF API Activity schema (one row per audit event; metadata.uid is the audit event ID). Purpose-built tools search and summarize it and look up identity, IP, service-account, cluster and allowlist context; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.summary: Someone outside the company used Jordan Doe's (jdoe@example.com) credentials to attack payments-prod on EKS, GKE and AKS. Every action came from 198.51.100.23. That IP is a known-malicious bulletproof VPS in the Netherlands (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING) that threat feeds tag for k8s API brute-forcing and for hosting an open Docker registry on port 5000. jdoe is on PTO (10-12 to 10-19) and normally uses macOS, but the client here was kubectl on Linux. The attacker ran the same playbook on each cloud: checked permissions, listed namespaces, failed to read kube-system secrets or create a kube-system job, then read payments-db-credentials and started a privileged pod (debug-tools-7f9c, hostPID/hostNetwork, host / mounted) in payments and exec'd into it. From the attacker IP it then used the cluster-admin argocd-application-controller service-account token (an in-cluster-only account that normally talks from 10.x addresses) to create the cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding 'jdoe-break-glass' for jdoe. As cluster-admin, the attacker set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet 'kube-metrics-agent' and a CronJob 'node-cert-rotate' (runs every 15 minutes), both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus a NodePort service on port 30080. It finished by listing secrets in every namespace (the alert), on AWS at 14:25, GCP at 15:01 and Azure at 15:34.

It matches the standard 'kubectl debug node' pattern, uses busybox from an approved registry, and sits inside normal SRE triage work. argocd-application-controller, external-secrets, cert-manager and coredns service accounts doing routine high-volume reads/updates of secrets and services from their expected in-cluster 10.x addresses. Only argocd use from 198.51.100.23 is malicious.
Many engineers doing namespaced get secrets/services and pods/exec into app pods from corp 203.0.113.x addresses with ordinary tooling.
03:05 ClusterRoleBinding updates by eks:addon-manager, aksService and system:addon-manager are managed-platform reconciliation.
Anonymous failed GETs from 198.18/15 addresses on all clusters are internet scanner noise; all were denied.
